body:
The Problem Facing Independent India

At the time of independence in 1947, the Indian subcontinent contained directly administered British Indian provinces as well as more than 560 princely states.

The princely states were ruled by hereditary rulers under British paramountcy. They were not administered in exactly the same manner as British Indian provinces. When British rule ended, this paramountcy lapsed, and the future relationship of the states with India or Pakistan had to be settled.

If numerous states remained outside the Indian Union, the resulting political fragmentation would create serious difficulties for national unity, administration, communications and security.

Patel and the States Department

Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel became independent India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister in August 1947. He also took responsibility for integrating princely states into India.

The States Department was established in June 1947 under Patel's leadership. V. P. Menon served as its Secretary and played an important role in negotiating arrangements with princely rulers.

Patel combined negotiation, persuasion and firmness in obtaining accession agreements and helping create a politically united country.

Accession and Integration

Instrument of Accession

An Instrument of Accession was a legal document through which a princely ruler agreed to join a dominion on specified subjects. Under the standard arrangements for accession to India in 1947, these subjects included defence, external affairs and communications.

Accession and merger were not identical. Accession established a formal political relationship with India on specified matters. Subsequent merger agreements and administrative arrangements brought many states into closer political and administrative union.

The process was not completed through one document or one method. Some rulers agreed readily, while others resisted or demanded special arrangements.

Junagadh: A Major Gujarat Example

The princely state of Junagadh, in the Saurashtra region of Gujarat, presented a serious accession problem. Its Nawab decided to accede to Pakistan, although there was strong opposition to that decision among people in the state.

Junagadh subsequently came under Indian administration. In a February 1948 plebiscite, an overwhelming majority of participating voters supported joining India.

A plebiscite is a direct vote by eligible people on an important public question. In the Junagadh case, it concerned the state's political future.

Hyderabad as a Contrasting Example

The princely state of Hyderabad, ruled by the Nizam, was another major challenge. It was integrated into India in September 1948 following Indian military action known as Operation Polo.

Junagadh and Hyderabad show why it is inaccurate to say that all princely states entered India peacefully, simultaneously or through identical procedures.

Prelims focus

  • There were more than 560 princely states at independence.
  • States Department: Formed in June 1947 under Patel.
  • V. P. Menon: Secretary of the States Department.
  • Junagadh: February 1948 plebiscite favoured India.
  • Hyderabad: Integrated in September 1948 following Operation Polo.
  • Trap: An Instrument of Accession and a subsequent merger were not the same legal or administrative step.

[Sources: Government of India, Press Information Bureau, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel: The Man Who United the Nation, 30 October 2021, pp. 2–4, sections on the States Department, Junagadh and Hyderabad; Government of India, Employment News, “Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and National Unity”, section “The Master of Statecraft”, 2022. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: States Department leadership, accession on three subjects, later merger and consolidation, and the dated Junagadh and Hyderabad cases.
pictures.caption: Accession was an initial legal step; wider integration required further political and administrative arrangements.

title: Sardar Patel and the Integration of Princely States after Independence

body:
National Unity Required Effective Administration

For Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, political integration was not sufficient by itself. A newly independent country also needed an administration capable of maintaining public order, implementing laws and delivering essential services across its territory.

His earlier experience in the Ahmedabad municipality and in organizing Gujarat's mass movements had shown the value of disciplined workers, reliable information, clear responsibilities and practical decision-making.

The Role of All India Services

Patel strongly supported the development and protection of the All India Services, particularly the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and the Indian Police Service (IPS).

These services were intended to provide professionally trained officers who could work in both Union and state administration, helping maintain administrative continuity and common standards across India.

All India Service

An All India Service is a service whose officers belong to state or joint cadres and serve under both Union and state governments. The IAS and IPS are important examples.

Patel believed that such officers should be able to perform their duties with integrity, professional competence, impartiality and courage. They needed sufficient security to give frank advice instead of changing their professional judgment merely to satisfy political pressure.

The Steel Frame of India

The expression steel frame describes the role of a stable and competent civil service in supporting the functioning of government. Although the expression had earlier associations with the colonial Indian Civil Service, Patel emphasized the need for professional services loyal to independent India's constitutional order.

In the Constituent Assembly on 10 October 1949, Patel defended the importance of strong All India Services for preserving India's unity.

His position did not mean that civil servants should govern independently of elected representatives. The intended distinction was between political responsibility, exercised through the constitutional government, and professional administrative duty, performed lawfully and impartially by public officials.

Continuity between His Gujarat Work and National Role

Patel's approach to public administration can be understood through 3 connected experiences:

  1. Municipal service: Sanitation, water supply and local civic management required practical implementation.
  2. Mass movements: Kheda, Borsad and Bardoli required organization, communication and discipline.
  3. National administration: Integration of states and protection of professional civil services required cooperation among diverse regions and institutions.

Prelims focus

  • Patel strongly supported the All India Services.
  • IAS: Indian Administrative Service.
  • IPS: Indian Police Service.
  • 10 October 1949: Patel defended All India Services in the Constituent Assembly.
  • Important principles included integrity, impartiality, professional advice and administrative continuity.
  • Trap: All India Services are not services meant only for the Union government; their officers serve within Union and state administrative arrangements.

[Sources: Government of India, Press Information Bureau, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel: The Man Who United the Nation, 30 October 2021, final section on All India Services; Government of India, Employment News, “Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and National Unity”, section “The Creation of All India Services”, 2022; Press Information Bureau, “Sardar Patel: Organiser par excellence”, sections on municipal administration and public service, 2016. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Patel’s All India Services connect constitutional government with Union and state administration, supporting continuity and national unity.
pictures.caption: Patel linked professional administration with constitutional government and national unity.

title: Sardar Patel's Administrative Thought and the All India Services

body:
Compare the Major Movements by Their Immediate Grievances

Several important campaigns in Gujarat used nonviolent public resistance, but they did not arise from the same cause. The most reliable way to distinguish them is to identify what was being contested, who participated and which leader organized the response.

MovementYearImmediate issuePrincipal association
Ahmedabad1918Textile wages and withdrawal of plague bonusGandhi; Anasuya Sarabhai
Kheda1918Land-revenue demand after crop failureGandhi; Vallabhbhai Patel
Borsad1923–1924Additional punitive police taxVallabhbhai Patel
Bardoli192822% increase in land-revenue assessmentPatel; title Sardar
Dandi1930Colonial salt tax and government monopolyGandhi; Salt March

The Distinctions Behind These Facts

Labour and Agricultural Movements

Ahmedabad concerned a dispute between workers and mill owners about wages. Kheda concerned agricultural cultivators seeking suspension of land-revenue collection after a poor harvest. The participation of Gandhi in both movements does not make their causes identical.

Four Different Tax-Related Grievances

Kheda: The existing land-revenue demand remained difficult to meet because agricultural production had fallen.

Borsad: An additional punitive police levy was imposed on the population.

Bardoli: The agricultural land-revenue assessment was increased by approximately 22%.

Dandi: Gandhi deliberately broke a law governing salt production as a challenge to the colonial salt monopoly and tax.

Gandhi and Patel: Different but Connected Roles

Gandhi provided the broader philosophy of satyagraha and led major campaigns such as the Ahmedabad workers' struggle, Kheda and the Dandi March. Patel developed an especially important role in village-level organization and direct leadership of the Kheda, Borsad and Bardoli movements.

After independence, Patel's experience as an organizer and administrator was applied to the integration of princely states and the development of a stable national administration.

Essential Chronology

Keep these pairs separate

  • Porbandar and Rajkot: Gandhi's birthplace and childhood home.
  • Kochrab and Sabarmati: Gandhi's first Indian ashram in 1915 and its later location from 1917.
  • Kheda and Bardoli: Revenue suspension after crop failure and resistance to a 22% revenue increase.
  • Borsad and Bardoli: Punitive police tax and increased agricultural land revenue.
  • Sabarmati and Dandi: Starting point and destination of the 1930 Salt March.
  • Accession and merger: Initial political joining and subsequent wider administrative integration of princely states.

How the Gujarat Experience Connected to National Independence

The Gujarat campaigns demonstrate a sequence in the development of organized public action. Gandhi used satyagraha in industrial and agricultural disputes, maintained institutions devoted to constructive work and connected a local act at Dandi to a national civil-disobedience campaign.

Patel's experience showed how disciplined local organization could support mass participation. His later role in integrating princely states and protecting professional administration linked the struggle for independence with the task of governing a united country.

Prelims focus

  • 1915: Kochrab Ashram; 1917: shift to Sabarmati.
  • 1918: Ahmedabad workers' satyagraha and Kheda peasant satyagraha.
  • 1923–1924: Borsad's punitive police-tax protest.
  • 1928: Bardoli's revenue struggle and Patel's title Sardar.
  • 1930: Dandi Salt March and deliberate breach of the salt law.
  • 1947 onward: Patel's leadership in princely-state integration and national administration.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, “The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947”, pp. 115–121, 2020–21 printing; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, “Nationalism in India”, pp. 54–65; Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook: Anand, “Brief History of the District”, pp. 14–15; Press Information Bureau, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel: The Man Who United the Nation, 30 October 2021, pp. 1–4; Gandhi Heritage Portal, “Kochrab Ashram” and “Sabarmati Ashram”. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The sequence from Gandhi's first Ahmedabad ashram to Patel's nation-building role.
